cards.q: What is Syslog and over which port does it work?
cards.a: Syslog sends device log messages to a central syslog server over UDP 514; entries carry facility plus severity (0-7) and timestamps.

cards.q: What makes up a syslog message?
cards.a: A syslog message consists of facility (source of the event) plus severity (importance) plus the event text, with a timestamp; destinations can be console, buffer, or server.

cards.q: How does syslog severity numbering work?
cards.a: Severity ranges 0-7 where a lower number is more severe: 0 emergencies, 1 alerts, 2 critical, 3 errors, 4 warnings, 5 notification, 6 informational, 7 debugging.

cards.q: What are the syslog destinations and their commands?
cards.a: Console via logging console, on-box buffer via logging buffered, and server via logging host; SNMP traps can be sent via an NMS. Configure each separately.

cards.q: How do you configure the syslog server destination and level?
cards.a: Use logging host 192.0.2.10 to set the UDP server and logging trap informational to set the server level; logging source-interface Loopback0 sets the sender IP and logging timestamp datetime adds timestamps.

cards.q: What does the logging buffered command do?
cards.a: logging buffered 8192 stores log messages in an on-box ring buffer, separate from the server or console destinations.

cards.q: How does syslog differ from SNMP traps?
cards.a: Syslog is text logs over UDP 514 with numeric severity, while SNMP traps are structured alerts over UDP 162 using OIDs; syslog is for logs, SNMP for alerts.

cards.q: How do you view logged messages on a device and in a session?
cards.a: Use show logging to view the buffer/log, show logging | include 192 to filter, and terminal monitor to see log messages in the current terminal session.

cards.q: No logs arrive at the syslog server; what is the likely cause and check?
cards.a: Likely the trap/server level setting; check with show logging. Also check buffered config, clock for timestamps, firewall for UDP 514, and console level.

cards.q: Which syslog severity is the most severe?
cards.a: Severity 0 (emergencies) is the most severe; a lower number always means higher severity.

cards.q: Which command controls the level of logs sent to the syslog server?
cards.a: logging trap (e.g. logging trap informational) controls what goes to the server and can differ from the console level.

cards.q: How does device-buffered logging differ from server logging?
cards.a: Buffered logging is stored on-box via logging buffered and is separate from the server (logging host) or console destinations.
